story.title: Russia Conducts Parliamentary Elections Including Occupied Ukrainian Regions
story.summary: Russia is holding parliamentary elections for the first time in regions of Ukraine that it annexed during the ongoing conflict. The elections will fill 450 seats in the State Duma and 11 regional governorships, with only pro-Putin parties on the ballot. The vote is overshadowed by fears of mobilization and is characterized by a lack of genuine opposition.

event_overview.title: About Russia Elections
event_overview.subject: Russia Elections
event_overview.summary: Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election chooses the ninth convocation of the State Duma, the elected lower chamber of the Federal Assembly. Voting is being held during Russia’s war against Ukraine and alongside regional and municipal elections; the political environment has been marked by restrictions on opposition activity.

facts.label: Voting period
facts.value: Voting for the 2026 State Duma election is scheduled across three days, September 18–20, 2026; September 20 is the single voting day.

facts.label: Institution being elected
facts.value: The State Duma is the lower chamber of Russia’s Federal Assembly (parliament) and has 450 deputies.

facts.label: Electoral system
facts.value: The election uses a mixed system: 225 deputies are elected in single-member districts and 225 from federal party lists in proportional representation.

facts.label: Term and election authority
facts.value: State Duma deputies serve five-year terms. Under the federal election law, the president calls regular Duma elections, while election commissions administer the process under election legislation.

facts.label: Voter and candidate eligibility
facts.value: Russian citizens aged 18 or older may vote; a candidate for the State Duma must be at least 21 and permanently reside in Russia, subject to other legal qualifications and restrictions.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected timeline covers the opening of voting on September 18, 2026, rather than the full campaign, regional contests, vote count, certification, or longer-term political consequences.

explore_lenses.label: Why is voting in occupied areas disputed?
explore_lenses.title: International law and competing claims
explore_lenses.summary: Russia’s election commission has formally scheduled Duma voting in occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Ukraine, the UN and its partners say Russia has no lawful authority to hold elections there and that the annexation itself has no legal effect.

claims.text: Russia’s Central Election Commission ordered Duma elections on September 20, 2026, in the territories it calls the Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics and Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, where it says martial law is in force.

A UN official has said Russian-organized elections in occupied Ukrainian areas have “no legal grounds”; the position cites the General Assembly’s rejection of Russia’s attempted 2022 annexation as a basis for changing those regions’ status.
Ukraine’s Security Service describes the vote as illegal and says organizing or publicly calling for such elections in occupied territory can incur criminal liability under Ukrainian law.

explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground since annexation?
explore_lenses.title: Election is part of broader integration
explore_lenses.summary: The Duma vote is the first nationwide parliamentary election reported to include residents of the four regions Russia claimed in 2022. It follows measures documented by UN monitors to install Russian laws, citizenship rules and institutions in occupied territory.

claims.text: The September 18–20 vote is Russia’s first parliamentary election since its 2022 full-scale invasion to include residents of the four Ukrainian regions Moscow claimed to annex.

UN human-rights monitors report that Russian authorities in occupied territory have implemented Russian governance systems and laws, compelled residents to obtain Russian citizenship, and restricted expression.

A UN report based on more than 2,300 victim and witness interviews found that Russian authorities had imposed Russian language, citizenship, law, courts and education while suppressing Ukrainian identity and dismantling Ukrainian administrative systems.

Russia’s election commission presents the vote as an election held on territory it treats as part of the Russian Federation; Ukraine and the UN characterize the same process as an attempt to consolidate or legitimize occupation.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the three-day vote?
explore_lenses.title: Results, recognition and wartime conditions
explore_lenses.summary: Polling is scheduled to end on September 20, 2026, after which Russian authorities are expected to announce results for all 450 Duma seats. The ballot’s conduct and any claimed mandate in occupied areas are likely to remain contested rather than produce a diplomatic settlement.

claims.text: The election runs from September 18 through September 20 and fills all 450 State Duma seats; half are allocated from nationwide party lists and half from single-member constituencies.

AP reports that United Russia is widely expected to retain overwhelming control of the Duma, alongside other parties aligned with President Vladimir Putin; this is an expectation, not an official result.
The UN’s stated position is that such elections undermine prospects for peace, while Ukraine’s security service has urged residents of occupied territory not to participate.

story_report.summary: Russia is holding a three-day parliamentary election from September 18 to 20 that fills all 450 State Duma seats and, for the first time since its 2022 full-scale invasion, includes residents of four Ukrainian regions Moscow claims to have annexed. Only parties backing President Vladimir Putin and the war are on the ballot. The vote extends Russia’s electoral process into occupied territory, while its legal status and the conditions under which residents can participate remain contested.

sections.heading: Legal Status of Occupied Regions
sections.body: Russia’s Central Election Commission ordered Duma voting in the territories it calls the Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics and the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, where it says martial law applies. A UN official has said Russian-organized elections in occupied Ukrainian areas have no legal grounds, citing the General Assembly’s rejection of Russia’s attempted 2022 annexation. Ukraine’s Security Service calls the vote illegal and says organizing or publicly urging participation can carry criminal liability under Ukrainian law.

sections.heading: Russian Governance in Occupied Areas
sections.body: UN human-rights monitors say Russian authorities have established Russian governance systems and laws in occupied territory, compelled residents to obtain Russian citizenship and restricted expression. A separate UN report, based on more than 2,300 victim and witness interviews, found that Russian authorities imposed Russian language, citizenship, courts and education while suppressing Ukrainian identity and dismantling Ukrainian administrative systems. Russia’s election commission treats the territory as part of the Russian Federation, while Ukraine and the UN characterize the process as consolidating or legitimizing occupation.

sections.heading: Results and Participation Remain Pending
sections.body: Voting was still underway as of September 19, and final turnout, results, reported incidents and any post-election actions had not been established. United Russia is widely expected to retain overwhelming control of the Duma alongside other parties aligned with Putin, though that remains a forecast rather than an official result. The UN says such elections undermine prospects for peace, while Ukraine’s security service has urged residents of occupied territory not to take part.

unresolved.text: Independent access to occupied areas is limited, so public reporting cannot fully establish the extent to which residents are able to vote freely.
Final turnout, results, reported incidents and any actions taken after the election were not established while voting remained underway.

related_stories.summary: President Trump announced a new agreement with Denmark that he claims grants the United States 'permanent control over security' in Greenland.
